title: Morning Edition
dek: UN investigators say there are reasonable grounds to believe U.S. strikes in Iran amounted to war crimes while also finding crimes against humanity by Iranian authorities; South Sudan changes election leadership three months before its first planned national vote; South Korea builds a new Central Asian minerals partnership; and the Ideas desk asks whether morality can be decomposed into recurring social problems.

lead_story.headline: UN investigators say there are reasonable grounds to believe U.S. strikes in Iran amounted to war crimes
lead_story.summary: A UN-backed fact-finding mission says two U.S. strikes in Iran on February 28—on a primary school in Minab and a sports complex in Lamerd—were indiscriminate attacks that it has reasonable grounds to characterize as war crimes. The same mission says Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity during their crackdown on protests that began in December 2025.
lead_story.why_it_matters: The findings put alleged violations by both a foreign military and the Iranian state into one evidentiary record. They are conclusions of an independent UN-mandated fact-finding mission, not a court judgment. U.S. responsibility for Minab is supported by reporting on an internal military investigation; U.S. Central Command has denied carrying out the Lamerd strike, and the Pentagon has not released a final Minab investigation.
lead_story.original_language: English; Persian-language and UN material used in the underlying investigation

items.headline: South Sudan’s president dismissed the head of the election commission three months before the country’s first planned national vote
items.summary: President Salva Kiir removed National Elections Commission chair Abednego Akok Kacuol and named Gabriel Bol Deng Majok as his replacement. No public explanation accompanied the dismissal. The commission had only recently begun training state committees for voter registration ahead of elections scheduled for December 22.
items.why_it_matters: South Sudan has never held a national election since independence in 2011. Changing the leadership of the formally independent election body this late in an already compressed timetable raises questions about legal procedure, administrative continuity and whether registration and other preparations can be completed credibly.

items.headline: South Korea and five Central Asian states created a recurring summit focused on critical minerals, energy and supply chains
items.summary: Leaders from Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan met President Lee Jae Myung in Seoul for the first Korea–Central Asia summit. The meetings produced more than 70 agreements and memoranda and established a biennial leaders’ summit, with Kazakhstan due to host the next one in 2028.
items.why_it_matters: Critical-mineral strategy is increasingly about building processing, research and investment relationships rather than simply buying raw material. For South Korea, the summit broadens supply options; for Central Asian states, the important question is whether partnerships move beyond extraction into higher-value processing and technology.
items.original_language: English; Korean and regional primary material checked

items.headline: Congo’s Ebola outbreak crossed 2,500 deaths in August while response workers were running short of money and facing attacks
items.summary: On August 21, the UN’s senior Ebola coordinator said more than 2,500 people had died in the Democratic Republic of Congo’s Bundibugyo-virus outbreak and warned that available response funding was close to exhaustion. WHO data later confirmed continued expansion: by August 26, 5,794 cases and 2,786 deaths had been reported in Congo across six provinces.
items.why_it_matters: This became the largest Ebola outbreak ever recorded in Congo without dominating the international news cycle. The outbreak is unusually difficult because the Bundibugyo species has no licensed vaccine, transmission overlaps with conflict and displacement, and health workers themselves have been infected and attacked.

items.headline: Can morality be broken into a small set of recurring social problems?
items.summary: Oliver Scott Curry, Mark Alfano, Mark Brandt and Christine Pelican propose a framework of ‘moral molecules’: recurring combinations of basic cooperative concerns such as helping family, returning favors, coordinating groups, resolving conflict and respecting possession. The ambition is to explain why moral rules vary while still being built from a limited set of social ingredients.
items.why_it_matters: The framework offers a middle route between saying morality is universal in one fixed form and saying moral systems are incomparable products of culture. Its main challenge is reduction: a useful taxonomy of cooperative problems may describe many moral judgments without proving that cooperation is what makes them morally right.

items.headline: A village library in the French Pyrenees has started a weekly hour of stories for local children
items.summary: The library in Bedous, a small commune in the Aspe Valley, is holding Wednesday morning reading sessions through mid-October, with separate times for younger and older children. The program is free and organized through the local library and Haut-Béarn tourism network.
items.why_it_matters: Its stakes are exactly as small as they look: a village library making one recurring hour for children and stories. Recent Human Scale stops were East Java, rural Zimbabwe, Libreville and Aurora in the Philippines; Bedous moves the lane to a small European mountain community without turning it into national news or novelty.

worth_your_time.headline: What if many metaphysical disputes are problems created by our own conceptual rules?
worth_your_time.summary: Timothy Williamson reviews Amie Thomasson’s Rethinking Metaphysics, which argues that philosophers often mistake questions about how our concepts work for discoveries about a deep structure of reality. Williamson presses the central difficulty: claiming there are no deep metaphysical truths can itself begin to look like a deep metaphysical claim.
worth_your_time.why_it_matters: This is a dispute about what philosophy is for. If Thomasson is right, some famous metaphysical battles should be dissolved or redirected toward practical conceptual engineering. If Williamson’s objection lands, the attempt to deflate metaphysics may depend on exactly the kind of substantive metaphysical commitments it says we should stop making.
worth_your_time.country: United States / United Kingdom — analytic philosophy

editorial_review.triangulation_check: pass with explicit uncertainty — the Iran lead combines Reuters, AP’s independent investigation/reporting and the UN-mandated mission’s findings; Minab responsibility is supported but the Pentagon’s final investigation is unpublished, while CENTCOM disputes Lamerd. South Sudan combines AP with the election commission’s own current records and preparation statements. South Korea–Central Asia uses Reuters plus summit/official records. Congo combines contemporaneous Reuters reporting with WHO outbreak data. Claims that remain participant-dependent are attributed.
editorial_review.difference_from_recent: The paper moves from environmental health and military deconfliction toward accountability for wartime civilian harm, fragile election administration, resource diplomacy, an under-covered epidemic and two questions about how moral and metaphysical categories are built.
notes_for_next_edition: Iran war-crimes findings should return for release of the full evidentiary report, U.S. investigation results, a formal legal process or materially new evidence—not routine political reaction.
South Sudan election administration should return for voter-registration launch, a legal challenge, timetable change or evidence of operational disruption.
Korea–Central Asia should return when agreements become financed projects or produce concrete mineral-processing capacity.
Congo Ebola can return for a major epidemiological turn, new countermeasure, funding breakthrough or cross-border transmission—not routine cumulative counts.
Human Scale should rotate away from Western Europe next if a credible African, Latin American, Asian, Middle Eastern or island local source clears the bar.
